name: get_engine_info
description: Returns the engine's version, platform, launch settings and package status. Call it first, to check that the engine is new enough and to see which toolchain packages are downloaded. It is fast and local: it never uses the network. Missing packages are downloaded automatically by the tools that need them, unless auto_download is off.

inputSchema.title: GetEngineInfoInput
inputSchema.description: The get_engine_info tool takes no inputs.

outputSchema.title: GetEngineInfoOutput
outputSchema.description: The engine's version, platform, launch settings and package status.

engine_version.description:
The engine version: its release date, as yyyy.mm.dd (its release tag
is the same date as yyyy-mm-dd). Compare versions by date.

protocol_versions.description: The MCP protocol versions the engine accepts, newest first.

platform.description: The platform the engine runs on, such as darwin-arm64.

operating_system.description:
The operating system and its version, such as "macOS 26.5" or
"Windows 10.0.26100.2314", for system info; on Linux with the desktop
session when known, such as "Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, GNOME on Wayland".

engine_commit.description:
The commit the engine was built from, short (7 hex digits); omitted
for a build made outside a git checkout.

engine_folder.description:
The engine folder, as the host set it with the --engine-folder
command-line argument. The engine keeps its packages and logs there.

auto_download.description:
Whether the engine downloads and repairs packages automatically when a
tool needs them. On by default. The host turns it off with the
--no-auto-download command-line argument.

command_line.description: The command-line arguments the engine was launched with, as given.

log_file.description:
The log file this engine process writes, in the logs subfolder of the
engine folder. Useful when reporting a problem.

packages.description:
Every package the engine uses, from its remote config, with its
status. Empty until the engine has read its remote config (before
its first operation that needs packages).

remote_config.description: The engine's remote config: where its package releases come from.

boards_schema.description:
The address of the board schema this engine reads (Logix Catalog's):
the JSON Schema of each board file, in the catalog and in custom
boards folders, which may name it in a "$schema" key so editors can
check them. A file that names another schema is refused.

catalog.description: The board catalog the engine reads: its Logix Catalog version.

hdl_extensions.description:
The file extensions of the HDL files the tools take, without the
dot, so a frontend knows which files are sources: source (design
and testbench files: v, sv) and include (files they include: vh,
svh). Pin files are per FPGA family: get_catalog's families give
each its constraint_extension and constraint_comment.

language_server.description:
Verible's Verilog language server, for a host that runs it itself
for live errors and other help while the user types: the command
(its absolute path), its arguments and the environment variables to
set for it, on top of the host's own (none today). Its arguments
check syntax only (Verible's style rules would flood beginners;
lint finds design problems) and turn hover info on. Omitted until
the FPGA tools (logix-core) are downloaded.

developer_settings.description:
The developer settings in effect: the environment variables the
engine reads for development and diagnostics (LOGIX_ENGINE_CHANNEL,
LOGIX_ENGINE_DEV_REMOTE_CONFIG, LOGIX_ENGINE_DEV_CATALOG_FOLDER), each
with its value, when set. Omitted when none is, as for users.

versions.description:
The version tree, for system info: the engine, its packages under
it, and under logix-core the third-party releases it bundles. A
frontend shows it under its own entry (see Show system info in the
tool API's recipes).

report.description:
The engine's system info for people, as plain text (for bug reports,
when the engine is the product people use, such as with an AI
agent): the version, operating system, log file, engine folder,
automatic download and command line, then the developer settings
when any is set, then the version tree. Show it as is; its wording
can change in any version, so programs read the fields above.

description: Deprecated: call check_updates instead. Without packages and force, this is the same as check_updates with cached_config_ok: it downloads or repairs the engine's toolchain packages, reading the remote config first when the saved one is more than 24 hours old, and check_only downloads nothing and says what would download. Download nothing: only read the remote config when it's due and say

name: check_updates
description: Downloads and updates the engine's packages (the board catalog and the FPGA tools): reads the engine's remote config, downloads what it names that isn't downloaded yet (or is broken), and uses it from the next call. It's the only tool that moves the engine to newer releases: other tools download a missing or broken package of the releases in use, inside their own call, but never switch releases. cached_config_ok uses the saved remote config when it was read less than 24 hours ago, so the call is quick and works offline; without it, the config is read now. check_only downloads nothing and says what would download, with sizes. AI agents: before the first other call in a session, call this with cached_config_ok and check_only; when its to_download and updates are both empty, go on without mentioning it; otherwise download as a step of its own in your plan, telling the user how much (its summary says), by calling it again with cached_config_ok and without check_only, then show that call's summary lines. Also call it when the user asks for updates, to download ahead of time (such as before going offline), or when a tool returns a setup error with the download_packages action. It works even when automatic download is off. A download can take a few minutes; the tool reports progress and can be cancelled. When newer_engine is in the result, tell the user that a newer Logix Engine is available and give its page: the engine never updates itself.

cached_config_ok.description:
Use the saved remote config when it was read less than 24 hours ago,
instead of reading it now: quick, and works offline. The config is
read anyway when there's no saved one, or it's older. Use it when the
host starts and before an AI session's first call; leave it off when
the user asks for updates. Defaults to false.

check_only.description:
Download and switch nothing: only say what a call without it would
do, in to_download (with sizes) and updates. Quick: use it to tell
the user how much will download before downloading. It keeps the
saved remote config as it was, so call again with the same
cached_config_ok to download. Defaults to false.

name: get_catalog
description: Returns board and FPGA definitions from the engine's read-only catalog. Use it to find a board's catalog ID, such as icesugar-1-5, to pass as the board of other tools, or to see a board's FPGA and how it is programmed. Each section is returned only when asked for: {"boards": {"fetch": true}} returns all boards, and {"boards": {"fetch": true, "ids": ["icesugar-1-5"]}} only the listed ones. Boards include those of the request's custom_boards_folder, marked custom, a custom board replacing the catalog board with its ID. The families section gives each FPGA family's name for people, the extension of its pin constraint files, their comment marker and the toolchain that builds it. Board descriptions are the boards' names for people; resources come with words for people (type_label, pins_text, notes_text), drive requirements with a text, and FPGAs with a label.

boards.description: Which boards to return. Omitted means none.

fpgas.description: Which FPGAs to return. Omitted means none.

families.description:
Which FPGA families to return, by ID, such as ice40 or gw1n.
Omitted means none.

custom_boards_folder.description:
The host's own boards: the absolute path of a folder of board files,
one board each in the catalog's format, named by board ID, such as
boards/my-board.json (a project's boards folder). board can name one
of them; one with a catalog board's ID replaces that board in this
request. Problems in any file come back as a request error with a
diagnostic for each, at file, line and column. Send the same folder to
every tool. Omitted means none.

display_paths.description:
How to name paths in what people read (diagnostics, messages,
testbench output, live tool output, diagram labels): files named as
a whole, then folders whose files keep their path below the folder
under the folder's new name ("" gives names relative to it); the
first match in each list wins. Paths are compared by real location.
Never applied to command lines or fields that are paths. Omitted
means paths read as the request gave them.

CatalogQuery.description: Selects entries from one catalog section.

fetch.description: Whether to return this section. Defaults to false.

ids.description:
Catalog IDs of the entries to return. Omitted means all entries. An
ID that isn't in the section is an error.

DisplayPaths.description:
How to name paths in what people read: diagnostics, messages, testbench
output, live tool output and diagram labels. Never command lines or
fields that are paths.

files.description:
Files named as a whole. They come before folders; the first that
matches wins.

folders.description:
Folders whose files keep their path below the folder, under the
folder's name `as`. The first that matches wins.

DisplayPath.description: One file or folder and how to name it.

path.description: The file or folder, as an absolute path.

as.description:
How people read it: any text. For a folder, a path inside it keeps
its part below the folder after this and "/", or alone when this is
empty, so "" gives names relative to the folder.

The standard dimensions, connection then memory, each with the values

resources.description:

colors, active), uart (tx, rx), pmod (its 8 signal pins), header,
and unclassified (every wired pin no other resource lists). A name
with one pin is a plain port, with several a vector, bit 0 first.
The order of resources means nothing. A resource's requires lists
what must be done for it to work, such as a jumper a clock needs (a
setup). For creating designs and pin files for the board, such as a
blinky. Omitted when none are known; a type a board doesn't list is unknown,
unless the board has an unclassified resource.

Hints for AI agents, and people, writing designs for the board: only
what its other fields can't express. Resources may have their own

name: simulate
description: Simulates one testbench with Icarus Verilog and opens its waveform in Open Logix's waveform viewer: compiles the design files with the testbench, runs it to write the waveform (.vcd) into the build folder, writes the viewer, a self-contained page with the waveform in it (page_file), and opens it in a window of its own (Logix Waveforms). The viewer shows the testbench's own signals, opens at the first failure, and saves the person's view as they change it, in view_file (<testbench>.view), unless save_view is false. name: diagram
description: Draws the design as schematic diagrams, one per module, as written: its other modules, the FPGA's own blocks and memories, and one block per signal the module's code drives (a register, or a block of logic), named after it, its inputs labeled with the signals it reads, with the wires between them; not the multiplexers and gates synthesis would make. The engine lays out and draws every module itself. Writes, in the build folder, diagram-<top_module>.html, one self-contained page with every module (double-click a module to open it, drag to pan, scroll to zoom, hover anything for its details; it needs no network or other software, so any web browser shows it), and in its diagram/ folder (replaced by each call) each module's SVG and diagram.json, a model of every module's blocks, ports, signals and source lines. It then opens the page in a window of its own (Logix Diagrams) for the person at the screen; if it can't, viewer_problem says why. Set open to false to only write it, such as when no one is at the screen or the host shows the page itself (page_file). List the design files; the engine doesn't search for them. For a testbench failure, the simulation time it happened at, in
nanoseconds, when known.

CommandRecord.description: One program the engine ran, with what it takes to run it again.

tool.description: The program's name, such as yosys.

package.description:
The package the program came from, with its version and the core's
tool, such as "logix-core 2026.11.10 (oss-cad-suite)". Omitted for a
program from elsewhere, such as a custom programmer command.

cwd.description: The folder it ran in, as an absolute path.

args.description:
The program as an absolute path, then its arguments, exactly as
passed.

shell.description:
One shell command line that runs it again the same way: in the same
folder, with the same minimal environment (PATH, the home and
temporary folders and, on Windows, the variables its programs need).

name: close_viewers
description: Closes windows this engine opened for the person at the screen (simulate, open_waveform and diagram, in Logix Waveforms and Logix Diagrams): one page's window, every window of one kind, or all of them. Never touches windows another engine opened. Views are saved as they change, so nothing is lost. The windows also close when the engine exits.

inputSchema.title: CloseViewersInput
inputSchema.description: Which windows to close; omitted fields mean all.

kind.description: The kind of page: "waveforms" or "diagram". Omitted means every kind.

page.description:
One page's window, by the page's path as the tool that wrote it
returned it (absolute, such as /home/user/proj/_build/main_tb.html).
Omitted means every page.

name: build
description: Builds an FPGA design into a bitstream: synthesizes the Verilog or SystemVerilog sources, places and routes them on the board's FPGA using the constraint file, which maps top-level ports to pins (.pcf for iCE40, .lpf for ECP5, .cst for Gowin, .xdc for Xilinx), and packs the bitstream into the build folder. Give the source files explicitly; the engine doesn't search for them, though `include files are found next to the including file or in the source folder. A build with no changes since the last one returns at once with up_to_date set. The first build may download the toolchain package first, which takes a few minutes. Design problems come back as a design error with diagnostics at file and line. Set lint to true to check the design with lint first, as an editor's Verify does: its problems join the build's in diagnostics, without repeats, and never stop the build. After a successful build, program_board programs the bitstream into the board.

board.description:
The target board's ID: a catalog ID such as icesugar-1-5 (get_catalog
lists them), or the ID of a board in custom_boards_folder.

board_variant.description:
The board variant: some or all of the selector of one of the board's
variants, which get_catalog lists, such as {"connection": "usb",
"memory": "ram"} or just {"memory": "ram"}. The board's first
variant with these values is used. Omitted or {} means its first
variant, its default.

custom_boards_folder.description:
The host's own boards: the absolute path of a folder of board files,
one board each in the catalog's format, named by board ID, such as
boards/my-board.json (a project's boards folder). board can name one
of them; one with a catalog board's ID replaces that board in this
request. Problems in any file come back as a request error with a
diagnostic for each, at file, line and column. Send the same folder to
every tool. Omitted means none.

display_paths.description:
How to name paths in what people read (diagnostics, messages,
testbench output, live tool output, diagram labels): files named as
a whole, then folders whose files keep their path below the folder
under the folder's new name ("" gives names relative to it); the
first match in each list wins. Paths are compared by real location.
Never applied to command lines or fields that are paths. Omitted
means paths read as the request gave them.

top_module.description: Name of the top-level module, such as main.

source_folder.description: The folder with the design files, as an absolute path.

source_files.description:
The HDL files to build (.v or .sv), relative to the source folder,
with / as the separator, such as ["main.v", "rtl/uart.v"]. Don't list
testbenches or included files.

constraint_file.description:
The constraint file, relative to the source folder: .pcf for iCE40,
.lpf for ECP5, .cst for Gowin, .xdc for Xilinx. Another extension is
refused, since each family's tools read only their own format.

build_folder.description:
Where the build writes its files, as an absolute path. One of its last
two folder names must contain "build", such as
/home/user/proj/_build. It may be inside the source folder but
can't be the source folder itself. It is created if needed.

defines.description:
Verilog macro definitions, from name to value, such as
{"USE_PLL": "", "WIDTH": "8"}. An empty value defines the macro with
no text, for `ifdef. SYNTHESIZE is always defined.

verbose.description:
Let the tools print more detail, shown in the live output and the
logs. It doesn't change the result. Defaults to false.

lint.description:
Check the design with lint (Verilator) first, as an editor's Verify
does: lint finds likely mistakes synthesis accepts and gives clearer
errors. Its problems never stop the build, which alone decides
success; they come first in diagnostics (and in a design error's
diagnostics), each with its tool, and a build problem on a line
lint already flagged with the same severity is left out. Defaults
to false.

debug_file.description:
A debug build: the Logix debugger inserted into the design, so a
host can watch and drive its nets on the board while it runs
(open_debug, read_debug, write_debug; docs/debugger.md). The debug
file, relative to the source folder, such as debug.toml: the nets to
watch and drive, by instance path from the top module (list_nets
lists them), and the clock the debugger runs on. The debugger talks
over the board's UART, so the design must not use its pins. The
sources are unchanged; the build writes debug_map.json next to the
bitstream and returns debug. Use a build folder of its own, such as
_build_debug, so a normal build keeps its own. Omitted means a
normal build.

VariantChoice.description:
A board variant in a request: some or all of a selector's values, such
as {"memory": "ram"}. The board's first variant with these values is
used, so {} means its first variant, its default.

connection.description: The connection, such as usb or ft232h. Omitted means any.

memory.description: The memory, flash or ram. Omitted means any.

DisplayPaths.description:
How to name paths in what people read: diagnostics, messages, testbench
output, live tool output and diagram labels. Never command lines or
fields that are paths.

files.description:
Files named as a whole. They come before folders; the first that
matches wins.

folders.description:
Folders whose files keep their path below the folder, under the
folder's name `as`. The first that matches wins.

DisplayPath.description: One file or folder and how to name it.

path.description: The file or folder, as an absolute path.

as.description:
How people read it: any text. For a folder, a path inside it keeps
its part below the folder after this and "/", or alone when this is
empty, so "" gives names relative to the folder.

bitstream.description: Path of the bitstream, relative to the build folder.

board_variant.description:
The board variant the build is for, by its full selector: the one
board_variant picked (the board's first with its values), which
program_board programs by default.

up_to_date.description:
True if nothing had changed since the last build, so nothing was
rebuilt.

resources.description:
Every resource the toolchain reports, sorted by name (ignoring
case): its own name, such as ICESTORM_LC or SLICE_LUTX, a short
description, how many are used and available, and the share used
(None when nextpnr's numbers aren't valid). Many are unused, on
Xilinx FPGAs most: a host shows the used ones first.

resources_summary.description:
The main resources in plain words, for showing to people without
knowing each FPGA family's names: the family's main capacity measure
first (logic cells or LUTs), then flip-flops, RAM blocks,
multipliers, PLLs and I/O pins, each the FPGA has, such as "27 of
7680 logic cells", with its share.

clocks_summary.description:
The design's clocks, each with a plain name, usually the design's
clock signal, such as "CLK" for the net CLK$SB_IO_IN_$glb_clk, the
net nextpnr reports, and the maximum frequency it can run at in MHz,
rounded to 0.01. A clock that misses its target isn't an error:
compare these with the design's needs.

report.description:
The report for people, the preferred way to show a build's resource
use to people, a line each: the main resource always, the
others when used, then each clock, such as "The design uses 27 of
7680 logic cells (1%)." and "Maximum clock speed: 194.4 MHz
(sys_clk).". Show it as is; its wording can change in any version.

report_summary.description:
The report in one line, for a status bar, such as "Uses 1% of
logic cells, max clock 194.4 MHz." Empty when there's nothing to
report.

diagnostics.description:
Every problem this call found, each with its tool: with lint, lint's
first, then the build's warnings, a build problem left out when lint
flagged the same line with the same severity; without lint, the
warnings.

checked_files.description:
The files this call read and checked, named as the request names
files: the listed files, the files they include and the constraint file. A host
replaces these files' earlier problems with this result's; other
files keep theirs. A design error has the same list in
data.checked_files.

commands.description:
The programs this call ran, in order, each with the exact command and
a shell line that runs it again without the engine, such as for a bug
report to the tool's developers.

debug.description:
For a debug build (debug_file): its debug map and what the debugger
watches and drives. Omitted for a normal build.

Selector.description:
Which of a board's variants: a value of each standard dimension. In a
board definition it says where the variant sits; in requests
(board_variant) it picks the variant with these values.

connection.description:
How the computer reaches the board: usb, bootloader, ft2232h,
ft232h, cmsis-dap, usb-blaster or unspecified (see the dimensions).

memory.description:
Where the design goes: flash (kept at power-off) or ram (lost at
power-off).

Resource.description:
One resource the toolchain reports, by its own name, with a short
description and how much the design uses.

name.description:
The toolchain's name, as nextpnr reports it, such as ICESTORM_LC or
SLICE_LUTX: what people search for and quote.

description.description:
What it is, in a few plain words, such as "Logic cell: a 4-input
LUT, a flip-flop and carry logic". None for a name the engine
doesn't describe yet.

used.description: How many the design uses, as nextpnr reports it.

available.description: How many the FPGA has, as nextpnr reports it.

percent.description:
The share used, in percent, rounded to 0.1. None when it can't be
computed or isn't valid: available is 0, or used is more than
available (nextpnr data the engine doesn't trust, as Apio's report).

display_percent.description:
The share for showing to people, in whole percent: the preferred
way to show the share to people. "0%" is guaranteed only when none
is used and "100%" only when all are used; anything else is rounded
up ("1%" for 27 of 7680, "99%" at most before all are used). None
when percent is.

ResourceSummary.description: One kind of FPGA resource, in plain words, with how much the design uses.

kind.description:
The kind: logic_cells, luts, flip_flops, ram_blocks, multipliers,
plls or io_pins. More kinds may be added.

label.description:
The kind in plain words, plural, such as "logic cells" or "LUTs", for
showing to people.

percent.description:
The share used, in percent, rounded to 0.1. None when it can't be
computed or isn't valid, as for resources.

display_percent.description: The share for showing to people, as for resources.

ClockSummary.description: One clock of the design, with a plain name and its maximum frequency.

name.description:
The clock's name for showing to people, usually the design's clock
signal, such as "CLK".

net.description: The clock net name nextpnr reports, the key in timing.

max_mhz.description: The maximum frequency the clock can run at, in MHz.

Diagnostic.description: A problem reported by a tool, at a file and line when known.

file.description: File, relative to the source folder, when known.

line.description: Line number, starting at 1, when known.

column.description: Column number, starting at 1, when known.

tool.description: Name of the tool that reported it, when known.

time_ns.description:
For a testbench failure, the simulation time it happened at, in
nanoseconds, when known.

CommandRecord.description: One program the engine ran, with what it takes to run it again.

tool.description: The program's name, such as yosys.

package.description:
The package the program came from, with its version and the core's
tool, such as "logix-core 2026.11.10 (oss-cad-suite)". Omitted for a
program from elsewhere, such as a custom programmer command.

cwd.description: The folder it ran in, as an absolute path.

args.description:
The program as an absolute path, then its arguments, exactly as
passed.

shell.description:
One shell command line that runs it again the same way: in the same
folder, with the same minimal environment (PATH, the home and
temporary folders and, on Windows, the variables its programs need).

DebugBuildInfo.description: A debug build's own result, build's debug.

debug_map.description: The debug map, relative to the build folder: debug_map.json.

build_id.description: The build ID the debugger reports, 8 hex digits.

debugger.description: The debugger's own share, synthesized alone.

net.description: The net, or a combined bus's list, as for watched nets.

members.description: A combined bus's members, most significant first.

offset.description: Its first bit in the write space.

format.description: The debug file's format for showing it (hex, dec or bin), if any.

enable_bit.description: Its bit in the override enables.

net.description:
The net in the design; for a bus combined from a list, the list,
as {main.a, pin.18}.

members.description: A combined bus's members, most significant first.

offset.description: Its first bit in the read space.

format.description: The debug file's format for showing it (hex, dec or bin), if any.

DebuggerUse.description:
The debugger's resources, from synthesizing it alone (an estimate:
placing it with the design can pack it a little differently).

luts_percent.description:
Each as a share of the FPGA's LUTs and flip-flops (on iCE40, its
logic cells, each of which has one of each), such as "8%": rounded
up, so "0%" only when none. Omitted when the build didn't report
them.

report.description:
For people, such as "The debugger uses about 460 LUTs (9%) and 250
flip-flops (5%) of the FPGA's 5280 logic cells."

name: clean_build
description: Deletes build folders. Given a build folder, such as /home/user/proj/_build, it deletes it. Given a folder of build folders, such as /home/user/proj/builds with one build folder per board, it deletes each build folder directly inside it, then the folder itself if nothing else is left. It only deletes folders the build tool made, so other files are never removed. A folder that doesn't exist is fine.

folder.description:
A build folder, or a folder whose direct subfolders are build
folders, as an absolute path. One of its last two folder names must
contain "build".

deleted.description:
The deleted folders, as absolute paths, including the given folder
when it was deleted. Empty when there was nothing to delete.

name: clean_logs
description: Deletes a host's old log session folders, by the policy the Logix Engine uses for its own logs. A host that keeps its logs in session folders (one folder per run, named <yyyymmdd>-<hhmmss>-<pid>, holding only .log files) calls it with its logs folder, such as /home/user/.myhost/logs, usually once at startup, and names its current session folder in keep. The newest 10 session folders are kept, at most 100 MB in all, none older than 30 days; folders changed in the last 24 hours (a program in them may still run), the ones in keep, and anything that isn't a session folder are never deleted. A logs folder that doesn't exist is fine.

logs_folder.description:
The host's logs folder, the parent of its session folders, as an
absolute path. Its last folder name must be "logs".

keep.description:
Session folders never to delete, as absolute paths, such as the
host's current session. Omitted means none beyond the policy's own.

deleted.description:
The deleted session folders, as absolute paths. Empty when there was
nothing to delete.

name: list_devices
description: Lists the USB devices connected to this computer, with their USB IDs, names and serial numbers, and for each the boards it may be: catalog boards and the request's custom_boards_folder, best first, each with the variants it fits and how well it matches: strong (very likely this board), possible (a few other boards look the same) or weak (many boards fit). Show the level as it is: how the engine decides it is internal and changes without notice. program_board needs the id of one of these devices. Given a build_folder, it lists only the devices that fit that build's board and variant, best first, each with its build_match: program the only one, or ask the user when there are several. Devices that need a driver or permissions first are listed apart, under unreachable, with the fix. On Windows, a device whose board's programmer needs a driver has driver: the one it needs (WinUSB), on which USB interface, the one it has and whether it's ready; on Linux, every device that fits a board has driver: its udev rule's state. Each device has who, its name for people, and driver has texts for people: its state, and the question to ask before install_driver (add) or uninstall_driver (remove). Give board, the user's chosen board, to name devices by it, list its devices first and get status: whether it's connected, in words for people (with build_folder, the build's board). When custom_boards_folder has a problem, the devices are still listed, against the catalog's boards only, and custom_boards_problem has the error.

inputSchema.title: ListDevicesInput
inputSchema.description:
Optionally, the host's own boards to match the devices against, besides
the catalog's, and a build whose board the devices must fit.

custom_boards_folder.description:
The host's own boards: the absolute path of a folder of board files,
one board each in the catalog's format, named by board ID, such as
boards/my-board.json (a project's boards folder). board can name one
of them; one with a catalog board's ID replaces that board in this
request. Problems in any file don't stop list_devices: the devices
are matched against the catalog's boards only, and
custom_boards_problem has the error every other tool returns (with
build_folder, they're a request error). Send the same folder to
every tool. Omitted means none.

display_paths.description:
How to name paths in what people read (diagnostics, messages,
testbench output, live tool output, diagram labels): files named as
a whole, then folders whose files keep their path below the folder
under the folder's new name ("" gives names relative to it); the
first match in each list wins. Paths are compared by real location.
Never applied to command lines or fields that are paths. Omitted
means paths read as the request gave them.

build_folder.description:
The build folder of a successful build, as an absolute path. When
given, only devices that fit the build's board in its variant are
listed (in devices and unreachable), each with build_match, best
first: the devices program_board can program that build into. The
build's board comes from its build record, custom boards included.

board.description:
The board the user has chosen, by ID, such as the one selected in a
frontend's toolbar (a catalog board, or one in
custom_boards_folder). When given, a device that may be it is named
as it in who and in the driver texts, and devices are listed in
this order: those that may be this board, then those that may be
other boards, then the rest (USB order within each). Without
build_folder only: with it, devices are listed best match first.
Omitted means no board.

DisplayPaths.description:
How to name paths in what people read: diagnostics, messages, testbench
output, live tool output and diagram labels. Never command lines or
fields that are paths.

files.description:
Files named as a whole. They come before folders; the first that
matches wins.

folders.description:
Folders whose files keep their path below the folder, under the
folder's name `as`. The first that matches wins.

DisplayPath.description: One file or folder and how to name it.

path.description: The file or folder, as an absolute path.

as.description:
How people read it: any text. For a folder, a path inside it keeps
its part below the folder after this and "/", or alone when this is
empty, so "" gives names relative to the folder.

devices.description:
The connected USB devices the engine can open, sorted by vendor ID,
product ID, bus and device number.

unreachable.description:
Devices the engine sees but can't open, so it can't program them or
read their names, and whose USB IDs fit a board: each with the fix,
such as permissions or a driver. Other devices it can't open are left
out.

status.description:
Only with board or build_folder: whether that board is connected, for
people and hosts, so every frontend says it the same way. code is
connected (one device may be it), several (more than one: ask the
user which), unreachable (none can be opened, but one that can't has
its USB IDs: action and the message say what makes it usable) or
not_connected (none); message says it in a sentence naming the
board, such as "The Alhambra II isn't connected. Connect it by USB,
then try again."; hints are more lines to show under it, a line
each (for not_connected: what is connected, and tips about the
cable and power); action is the suggested action, as in errors,
when there's something to do.

custom_boards_problem.description:
When custom_boards_folder has a problem: the error every other board
tool returns for it (a request error with a diagnostic for each
problem, at file, line and column). list_devices still lists the
devices then, matched against the catalog's boards only, so device
scans keep working while the user fixes the folder. With
build_folder, a problem is a request error, as in program_board.

other_serial_ports.description:
The USB serial ports the engine couldn't tie to a listed device,
sorted by vendor ID, product ID, interface and name: such as a
device that gives the serial port list another serial number than
its USB listing, two adapters without serial numbers that look the
same, or a device the engine can't open. Every USB serial port is
either here or in a device's serial_ports, so a host can always let
the user choose any of them (open_serial, without device). Omitted
when none.

Device.description: A connected device that the engine can open.

id.description:
The device's ID, to pass to program_board. Opaque: don't parse it.
It names the device on this computer for a short time: it stays
valid while the device stays on the same USB port, so list the
devices again before asking the user to choose.

label.description:
The device for people: its product name (else its manufacturer's
name, else "USB device"), then its manufacturer and USB IDs, such
as "Alhambra II v1.0A (AlhambraBits, 0403:6010)".

who.description:
The device for people in a sentence, for messages: "the Alhambra
II" when it may be only one board (or the request's board, when it
may be that one), else its label. Never the first of several boards
with its USB IDs.

vid.description: USB vendor ID, four lowercase hex digits.

pid.description: USB product ID, four lowercase hex digits.

manufacturer.description: The manufacturer name the device reports, when available.

product.description: The product name the device reports, when available.

serial_number.description: The serial number the device reports, when available.

release.description:
The device's release number (USB bcdDevice), four lowercase hex
digits, such as 0700; FTDI chips tell their type by it, and board
filters may require it. Reported so a pasted device listing says
everything a board request needs.

device.description:
USB device number on its bus. It changes when the device is plugged
in again.

boards.description:
The boards whose USB filters this device matches, best first. Empty
for a device that is no known board.

likely_boards.description:
The boards this device most likely is, best first: those of boards
at its strongest match level, unless that is weak (many boards fit,
so none is likely). Empty when no board is likely.

other_boards.description:
The other boards worth naming, after likely_boards, best first: the
rest of boards, except that when the device has a strong match, only
the request's board (board, else the build's) when the device may be
it, since dozens of boards that share a USB chip would only be
noise. Empty when there are none.

rank.description:
The device's place in one list of devices and unreachable together,
0 first: those that may be the request's board (board, else the
build's), then those that may be other boards, then the rest; within
each, devices before unreachable ones, each in its list's order. For
a host that shows both lists as one.

build_match.description:
How well the device matches the given build's board in the build's
variant: strong, possible or weak, as in boards. Present only when
list_devices was given a build_folder.

driver.description:
What the device needs for its board's programmer (the build's board
when list_devices was given a build_folder, else its best match) and
what it has: on Windows a driver, for a board whose programmer needs
one; on Linux a udev rule, for every device that fits a board. Never
on macOS. ready false means install_driver first.

serial_ports.description:
The device's serial ports, such as COM5, /dev/cu.usbserial-A10 or
/dev/ttyUSB1, each with the USB interface it's on when the system
says, by interface: for open_serial. Empty when it has none, or
when another connected device with its USB IDs and no serial number
makes them impossible to tell apart.

serial_port.description:
The serial port of its board's UART, the one a Serial Monitor
opens: on the UART's usb_interface when the board's data gives it,
else the device's only serial port. The board is the build's
(build_folder), else board when the device may be it, else its only
likely board. Omitted when it can't be told: then ask the user, from
serial_ports.

oneOf.description: A USB device.

BoardMatch.description: A board a device may be.

board.description:
The board's ID: a catalog ID, or a custom board's ID when custom is
true.

custom.description:
True when the board is from the request's custom boards folder rather
than the catalog's.

variants.description:
The board's variants this device fits, in the board's order, each
with its own match level. Use the level of the variant you mean,
such as the build's.

VariantMatch.description: A variant of a board that a device fits.

selector.description:
The variant's selector, such as {"connection": "usb", "memory":
"flash"}, as board_variant gives it in requests.

match.description:
How well the device matches the board in this variant: strong,
possible or weak. See MatchLevel.

Selector.description:
Which of a board's variants: a value of each standard dimension. In a
board definition it says where the variant sits; in requests
(board_variant) it picks the variant with these values.

connection.description:
How the computer reaches the board: usb, bootloader, ft2232h,
ft232h, cmsis-dap, usb-blaster or unspecified (see the dimensions).

memory.description:
Where the design goes: flash (kept at power-off) or ram (lost at
power-off).

MatchLevel.description:
How well a device matches a board, by what it means for the user, not
by its cause. The criteria are internal to the engine and change
without notice, so hosts must not infer why a device matched; they may
only show the level and compare levels (weak < possible < strong). No
level proves which board is connected.

oneOf.description: The device fits the board, but so do many other boards.

The device could be the board, but a few other boards look the
same.
The device is very likely the board.

DriverStatus.description:
What a device needs for a board's programmer, and what it has: a driver
on Windows (for devices whose board's programmer needs one), a udev rule
on Linux (for every device that fits a board). Not on macOS.

needed.description:
What the board's programmer needs: winusb (Windows) or udev-rule
(Linux).

interface.description:
On Windows, the USB interface that needs it, such as 0 (an FTDI
chip's first channel; its other channels, such as a serial port,
keep their driver). Omitted on Linux: a rule is for the whole
device.

current.description:
On Windows, the driver Windows has on that interface now, by its
service name in lowercase, such as ftdibus (FTDI's), usbser or
winusb. On Linux, the file of Logix Engine's udev rule for the
device's USB IDs, such as 70-logix-engine-0403-6010.rules, when
there is one (another rule may give access too). Omitted when there's
none.

Whether the programmer can use the device as it is. On Windows: true

name: program_board
description: Programs the bitstream of a successful build into the board it was built for. It doesn't build: call build first, and program_board only if the build succeeded. The board comes from the build, so it takes the build folder and the device to program: the id of a device from list_devices whose boards include the build's board (ask the user when several do). On ECP5, Gowin and Xilinx boards it first reads the connected FPGA's ID code and refuses a different FPGA, such as a board of another size than the build's, before writing anything. Most boards are programmed to flash, so the design stays after power-off.

name: install_driver
description: Windows and Linux. For a device from list_devices (in devices or unreachable) whose driver isn't ready, gives it what list_devices' driver says it needs. Ask the user first, saying what changes. On Windows: installs WinUSB, the driver the board's programmer needs, on the USB interface driver names; Windows then asks whether Logix Engine may make changes, and the user must answer Yes. Windows gives drivers by USB IDs and interface, not per board, so other connected devices with the same USB IDs get WinUSB too: the tool refuses while there are any, unless allow_same_ids is true (ask the user to unplug them, or to confirm). Vendor tools that use the interface (such as Vivado for a Digilent board) can't until uninstall_driver. On Linux: adds a udev rule that lets the user open devices with the board's USB IDs; the desktop then asks for the user's password. Where it can't (such as over SSH), the error's details have the commands the user can run in a terminal instead. Does nothing when the driver is ready already.

name: uninstall_driver
description: Windows and Linux. Undoes install_driver for a device from list_devices. Ask the user first. On Windows: removes every driver package libwdi installed for the board's USB interface (by WinUSB, and by Zadig with libusbK or libusb0 from older guides; never Windows' or a vendor's), the certificates libwdi signed them with, then asks Windows to look for drivers again, so the device gets Windows' own choice back (such as FTDI's, for vendor tools); Windows asks whether Logix Engine may make changes. On Linux: removes Logix Engine's udev rule for the device's USB IDs (never another rule); the desktop asks for the user's password. It applies to every device with the same USB IDs. Does nothing when there's nothing of Logix Engine's to remove.

inputSchema.title: UninstallDriverInput
inputSchema.description: The device, and how to tell its board.

device.description: The device's id from list_devices, in devices or unreachable.

custom_boards_folder.description: The host's own boards, as for list_devices. Omitted means none.

build_folder.description:
A successful build's folder, as for install_driver. Omitted means
the device's best match.

board.description:
The board the user has chosen, by ID, as for list_devices: names
the device in messages (who, summary) when it may be that board.
Omitted means none.

display_paths.description: How to name paths in what people read. Omitted means as given.

DisplayPaths.description:
How to name paths in what people read: diagnostics, messages, testbench
output, live tool output and diagram labels. Never command lines or
fields that are paths.

files.description:
Files named as a whole. They come before folders; the first that
matches wins.

folders.description:
Folders whose files keep their path below the folder, under the
folder's name `as`. The first that matches wins.

DisplayPath.description: One file or folder and how to name it.

path.description: The file or folder, as an absolute path.

as.description:
How people read it: any text. For a folder, a path inside it keeps
its part below the folder after this and "/", or alone when this is
empty, so "" gives names relative to the folder.

device.description: The device's id now (it can change with its driver).

who.description: The device for people in a sentence, as list_devices' who.

driver.description:
The device's driver now, as Windows reports it after looking again;
it may take a moment more to settle.

removed.description:
What was removed: on Windows, the driver packages, by their names in
Windows (oem<N>.inf); on Linux, the udev rule's file. Empty when there
was nothing, so nothing was done.

summary.description:
What was done, for people, a sentence each, such as "Added a udev
rule for the Alhambra II." or "Removed the WinUSB driver for the
Alhambra II." and "Windows uses its original driver again.".

DriverStatus.description:
What a device needs for a board's programmer, and what it has: a driver
on Windows (for devices whose board's programmer needs one), a udev rule
on Linux (for every device that fits a board). Not on macOS.

needed.description:
What the board's programmer needs: winusb (Windows) or udev-rule
(Linux).

interface.description:
On Windows, the USB interface that needs it, such as 0 (an FTDI
chip's first channel; its other channels, such as a serial port,
keep their driver). Omitted on Linux: a rule is for the whole
device.

current.description:
On Windows, the driver Windows has on that interface now, by its
service name in lowercase, such as ftdibus (FTDI's), usbser or
winusb. On Linux, the file of Logix Engine's udev rule for the
device's USB IDs, such as 70-logix-engine-0403-6010.rules, when
there is one (another rule may give access too). Omitted when there's
none.

ready.description:
Whether the programmer can use the device as it is. On Windows: true
with WinUSB, and with libusbK or libusb0, which older guides
installed. On Linux: whether the engine can open the device. False
means install_driver first.

label.description:
For people, what the device needs, in a sentence: "the WinUSB
driver" or "a udev rule". The texts below are for people too, the
same for every frontend; none names a frontend, its menus or its
buttons (crate::driver_texts).

state.description:
The device's state, such as "Driver: needs WinUSB on USB interface 0
to program the board (it has FTDI's driver now)." or "Access: ready
to program the board.".

tag.description:
A short tag while it isn't ready, for a list: "no driver yet" or "no
udev rule yet".

current_label.description: On Windows, current's driver for people, such as "FTDI's driver".

can_add.description: Whether install_driver has something to do: the device isn't ready.

can_remove.description:
Whether uninstall_driver may have something to remove: on Linux,
Logix Engine's rule is there (current); on Windows, the device has a
libusb driver (uninstall_driver says when none was libwdi's).

add.description:
When can_add: the question to ask before install_driver, and its
status and cancel lines.

remove.description: When can_remove: the same before uninstall_driver.

Consent.description:
A question to ask the user before a change (adding or removing a
driver or udev rule), and the lines to show around it: a frontend shows
it in its own dialog, with its own Cancel.

title.description: The question's title, such as "Install the board's USB driver?".

lead.description: One sentence: what it's for, naming the board.

steps.description:
What happens, a short sentence each, such as Windows' or Linux's own
permission prompt.

note.description: An optional last line, such as that it can be undone.

confirm.description: The label of the button that agrees, such as "Install Driver".

busy.description:
A status line while the change runs, such as "Installing the
board's driver…".

cancelled.description:
The line to show when the user declines, such as "Cancelled: the
driver wasn't installed.".

name: open_serial
description: Opens a serial port, such as a board's UART over its USB cable, for a Serial Monitor or an AI agent checking what a design prints, and returns a session: read it with read_serial, send with write_serial, end with close_serial. Take the port from list_devices: a device's serial_port is its board's UART (else choose from its serial_ports). Give device too (its id): then the session pauses while program_board writes that board and reopens after, and reopens the port when the board is plugged in again, even under another name. The format is 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit; baud defaults to 115200. The session stays open until close_serial or the engine exits.

port.description:
The port, such as COM5, /dev/cu.usbserial-A10 or /dev/ttyUSB1: a
device's serial_port or one of its serial_ports from list_devices.

device.description:
The device the port belongs to, by its id from list_devices, so the
session pauses while program_board writes it and finds the port
again after it's unplugged. Omitted means the port alone.

session.description: The session's ID, for the other serial tools.

name: read_serial
description: Returns the bytes a serial session received since the last read, exactly, as hex (two digits per byte), and what happened to its port meanwhile (paused for program_board, resumed, disconnected, reconnected). With wait_ms it waits up to that long for something to arrive (with until, for those bytes, such as 0d0a, a line ending); without, it returns at once. A Serial Monitor calls it in a loop with a wait, such as 1000 ms. Up to 1 MB is kept unread; beyond, the oldest is dropped (an overflow event).

wait_ms.description:
How long to wait for data, in milliseconds, at most 60000. Defaults
to 0: return what there is now.

until.description:
Bytes to wait for, as hex, such as "0d0a" (a line ending): wait
until what's received contains them (or wait_ms ends), instead of
returning at the first data.

hex.description:
What arrived, exactly: two lowercase hex digits per byte, such as
"48690d0a" for "Hi" and a carriage return and line feed. Empty when
nothing did. The engine passes bytes through unchanged, as a UART
does: decoding them (such as UTF-8 text) is the client's.

events.description: What happened to the port, in order. Omitted when nothing.

open.description: Whether the port is open now (false while paused or unplugged).

port.description: The port's name now: it may change when the board comes back.

SerialEvent.description: Something that happened to a session's port, in the order it happened.

kind.description:
What happened: paused (program_board is writing the board, so the
port is closed), resumed (reopened after that), disconnected (the
port went away, such as the board being unplugged), reconnected
(reopened when it came back), or overflow (data arrived faster than
it was read, and the oldest was dropped).

message.description:
The same for people, such as "Closing the serial port while the
board is programmed.".

name: write_serial
description: Sends bytes to a serial session's port, exactly as given, as hex (two digits per byte, such as 48690a for "Hi" and a line feed): any byte, text or not. Encoding text (such as UTF-8, and the line ending the device expects) is the client's. While the port is closed (paused or unplugged), nothing is sent and it's an error.

hex.description: The bytes to send, two hex digits each, such as "48690a".

name: close_serial
description: Ends a serial session and closes its port, so other programs can open it. What it received but wasn't read is dropped.

name: list_nets
description: Lists the nets of a design that a debug file can watch or drive: each named net of the top module after the design is read and flattened, with its path as debug files name it (from the top module, such as top.u_counter.count), its width in bits and its kind (input, output or inout for the top module's ports, internal otherwise). It only reads and elaborates the design (no synthesis), so it is quick. The board is needed for its FPGA's cell library.

board.description: The target board's ID, as for build.

board_variant.description: The board variant, as for build.

custom_boards_folder.description: A folder of custom boards, as for build.

source_folder.description: The absolute folder the source files are in.

source_files.description: The design's Verilog files, relative to source_folder.

VariantChoice.description:
A board variant in a request: some or all of a selector's values, such
as {"memory": "ram"}. The board's first variant with these values is
used, so {} means its first variant, its default.

connection.description: The connection, such as usb or ft232h. Omitted means any.

memory.description: The memory, flash or ram. Omitted means any.

path.description: Its path as debug files name it, from the top module.

kind.description: input, output or inout for a port of the top module; internal otherwise.

name: open_debug
description: Opens a debug session with the Logix debugger on a board, for a build made by build with debug_file and programmed with program_board. Give the build folder (its debug_map.json names the nets) and the board's serial port (a device's serial_port from list_devices). Give device too (its id from list_devices): then the session finds the port again when the board is plugged back in, even under another name. Checks that the board runs that very build, by its build ID, and refuses another. Opening releases every override, so the design runs on its own. The debugger owns the port while the session is open: don't open a serial session on it too. program_board on the board pauses the session, which reconnects after and checks the build again.

build_folder.description: The debug build's folder, as an absolute path.

port.description: The serial port, such as /dev/cu.usbmodem1102 or COM5.

device.description:
The device the port belongs to, by its id from list_devices, so the
session finds the port again after the board is unplugged, even
under another name. Omitted means the port alone.

session.description: The session's ID, for the other debug tools.

device.description: The device given, whose port the session follows.

build_id.description: The build ID the board's debugger reported, which matches the map.

drive.description: What can be driven: each driven net's name and width.

watch.description: What can be watched: each watched net's name and width.

format.description: For watched nets: the debug file's format for showing it.

name: read_debug
description: Reads nets of the running design through a debug session, all in one snapshot taken in a single clock cycle. Give the watched names to read (from open_debug), or none for all. Each value comes as bits (most significant first), as hex and, up to 53 bits, as a number.

names.description: The watched nets to read, by name. Omitted means all.

value.description: The value as a number, when it has 53 bits or fewer.

hex.description: The value in hex, such as 0x5b8d7f.

name: write_debug
description: Drives a net of the running design through a debug session: one of its drive names from open_debug. Writing takes the net over from the design until release; release gives it back. The value is a number, or a string in hex (0x..), binary (0b..) or decimal, and must fit the net's width. pulse, for a one-bit net, flips its value for one clock, whether it is driven or released, and leaves it as it was.

name.description: The net to drive, by its name in the debug file's drive list.

value.description: The value to drive. Required unless release is true.

release.description: Give an override net back to the design. Defaults to false.

pulse.description:
For a one-bit net: flip its value for one clock, driven or released,
then leave it as it was. Defaults to false.

driven.description: True while the debugger drives the net.

hex.description:
The value the debugger drives, read back from it, in hex; omitted
when it doesn't drive the net.

name: close_debug
description: Ends a debug session: releases every override, so the design runs on its own, and frees the serial port.

released.description:
False when the overrides couldn't be released, such as with the
board unplugged.

name: open_debug_panel
description: Opens an interactive panel for a debug session in the browser: it shows the watched nets live (as hex, decimal and bits) and has controls to drive each driven net and release it. Logix Engine serves it on this computer only, at 127.0.0.1, with a random token in its address. The panel uses the same session as read_debug and write_debug, so both can be used at once. Returns the address; with open false it only returns it, such as for a host that shows pages itself.

open.description: Open the panel in the default browser. Defaults to true.

url.description:
The panel's address. It works while Logix Engine runs, for any open
session (the page can switch between them).

opened.description: True when the browser was asked to open it.
